extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of crowd psychology, political leaders and commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic and descriptive principles about the psychology, behaviour, and influence of crowds and their leaders, as presented in a late-19th-century treatise. Useful for understanding how leaders address crowds, how assemblies behave, and the sociopolitical consequences of mass psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders follow public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader is seldom in advance of public opinion; almost always all he does is to follow it and to espouse all its errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect leaders to lead opinion in many colonial or political matters; much of a leader's influence derives from following prevailing public sentiment rather than from original insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader must comprehend crowd psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: To make skilful use of resources a leader must have arrived at a comprehension, at least in an unconscious manner, of the psychology of crowds, and must know how to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective leaders understand crowd mechanisms (suggestibility, emotions) and adapt speech/content accordingly; mastery need not be explicit but must shape rhetoric and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of striking terms and vivid images
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, phrases, and images must be chosen so as to evoke very vivid images; striking terms exercise a prodigious influence on the imagination of a pure democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoric that conjures concrete, alarming or memorable images (e.g., metaphors of vessels carrying people to 'fever-haunted lands') makes audiences feel personally threatened or implicated and thereby persuades them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence of energetic affirmations without proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A special description of eloquence, composed of energetic affirmations—unburdened with proofs—and impressive images, accompanied by very summary arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, forceful assertions and declamatory style are more effective on crowds than long chains of proof; leaders benefit by making confident statements rather than complex arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indulge in improbable exaggerations and violent affirmations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is all to the interest of the leaders to indulge in the most improbable exaggerations; the affirmation is never too violent, the declamation never too threatening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration and hyperbole intimidate audiences into silence or acquiescence (protesters risk being labeled traitors); such rhetorical excesses are strategic tools for gaining obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow intellect plus strong conviction often trumps erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence and high education often do more harm than good to leaders because nuance and explanation blunt the intensity and violence of conviction needful for apostles; great leaders have often been of narrow intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders who present simple, uncompromising convictions (even with limited intellectual subtlety) tend to attract and hold crowds more than those who display complex reasoning or excessive nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige outweighs arguments in assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parliamentary assembly the success of a speech depends almost solely on the prestige possessed by the speaker, and not at all on the arguments he brings forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers lacking prestige who present only arguments will generally be ignored; personal authority and reputation determine persuasive power in assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies can become crowds when excited
rubrics_metrics.description: When parliamentary assemblies reach a certain pitch of excitement they become identical with ordinary heterogeneous crowds, and their sentiments become extreme and unreflective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under excitement, assembly members lose individual self-consciousness and can vote or act against their own interests; this explains sudden collective excesses (e.g., revolutionary violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialists produce the best legislative work
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of good technical laws is a specialist who has prepared them in the quiet of his study; the law voted is the work of an individual and not of an assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation crafted by isolated experts is generally superior to laws produced by collective amendment processes; assemblies rely on specialists as temporary leaders to safeguard quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The work of a crowd is inferior to individual work
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of a crowd is always inferior, whatever its nature, to that of an isolated individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective decisions and creations tend to be less coherent and effective than those produced by competent individuals or specialists; crowds excel in enthusiasm but not in technical output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal dangers of parliamentary assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary assemblies present two serious dangers: (1) inevitable financial waste, and (2) progressive restriction of the liberty of the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These systemic risks arise from election-driven spending and from continual legislation that restricts freedoms and expands administrative power; they are inherent in representative institutions when influenced by mass suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral considerations lead to excessive public expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Deputies, victims of suggestion in their dread of their electors, will not venture to reject measures giving apparent satisfaction to democratic ideas (e.g., local railway grants, pensions), thus inflating budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vote-seeking behavior (approving local grants, expanded benefits) causes unsustainable public spending; individual deputies vote for visible short-term benefits despite long-term fiscal harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of laws restricts real liberty and empowers functionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase in dictatorial measures and regulations imposes constraints on citizens and forces acts formerly free; the proliferation of restrictive laws augments the number and power of functionaries who apply them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal overreach and administrative growth produce an impersonal, irresponsible administrative caste that becomes the true master of nations, producing de facto servitude despite apparent liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisations follow a lifecycle from crowd to decadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilisations progress from a crowd of mixed elements to a people with an ideal and institutions, then after reaching complexity they cease to grow and enter a phase of old age and decadence marked by loss of the founding ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of a unifying ideal leads to fragmentation into isolated individualities, weakening cohesion and making a civilisation vulnerable to decline and the resurgence of crowd-like characteristics.
